If you've been using the Fitbit app in recent years, you'll know that it's now been replaced by Google Health. (Google bought Fitbit back in 2019 .) The app will eventually replace Google Fit too, though we don't know exactly when that will be. Google has previously said it will happen before the end of the year .
While many features have been carried over into Google Health from its predecessors, some haven't. There have also been new additions, and a lot of rearranging has gone on too, so it can take a while to figure out exactly where everything is.
Whether you're a veteran from the Google Fit or Fitbit days, or you've just installed Google Health for the first time to use with a new device, these tips will help you explore everything the app has to offer and get the most out of it.
If you've been waiting to buy a device to track your steps before installing Google Health, you don't have to. You can still get the step-tracking features from the app, as long as you carry your phone with you on all your walks and runs.
Tap the Connections icon (top left), then Phone to start pulling in data from your Android or iOS smartphone. If you later add a wearable, you can switch to this for steps—or keep them both enabled (handy if you forget your tracker at home one day, for example).
The Today page is the first one you see when you open the Google Health app, so it makes sense to fill it with the stats that actually matter to you, rather than the metrics the app picks. Tap the pen icon just underneath the top bank of widgets to make changes.
You're able to switch between Standard view and Expanded view , depending on how much health and fitness information you want to see at once. In both views, you can swipe right or left to see more widgets.
Tap the + (plus) icon next to any widget you want to add to the Today page, and the - (minus) icon next to any widget you want to remove. Hiding widgets doesn't do anything to your fitness data, it just means that data isn't shown on the Today view.
You don't have to rely on your fitness tracker, smartwatch, or phone to capture all of your movement. To add something manually, tap Log on the Today view, then Activity , and pick the activity type—like Walk , Basketball , Indoor climbing , or whatever it is.
The app asks you to fill out key details, like the start and end points of the activity, before saving the record. You can manually add lots of other information from the same screens, from the hours you’ve slept to the meals you've had.
There are various parts of the Google Health interface, including the widgets on the Today page, where you'll see references to your health and fitness goals. These aren't going to be all that useful to you if you just leave the default values in place.
To make these metrics more meaningful, tap your profile picture (top right), then choose Google Health settings > Activity . You'll find numerous goals listed here, together with a few other settings, like whether or not to detect activities automatically.
Tap on any goal to set it or edit it. These targets affect the layout of screens throughout the app, and you might get notifications about them too, from time to time—if you don't want this, choose Manage notifications from the Activity screen.
You'll of course want your fitness tracker or smartwatch to be logging everything as accurately as possible. Even if the step counts are only off by a little each day, that can add up to a big difference over the weeks and months.
There are two settings to check here: If you tap your profile picture (top right), then choose Google Health settings > Activity , you can set your Stride length . This lets you give Google Health more precise measurements for your gait, whether walking or running.
Second, tap the Connections icon (top left), then your wearable. Choose Device preferences, and you can tell the app which wrist your wearable is usually on, which should mean more accurate step and movement tracking.
You may have seen mentions of Google Health Premium in the app or seen pop-ups about it, but what exactly is it? And what do you get for your money? The subscription replaces the old Fitbit Premium and works along similar lines.
For $10 a month, you get personalized and adaptable health plans that give you specific instructions for reaching your health and fitness goals. You also get a Gemini-powered AI Coach that gives you workout recaps and fitness advice based on the metrics you're recording.
The sleep summaries are more detailed in terms of sleep stages and the sleep scoring system. You also get access to a library of guided workouts and mindfulness sessions in the app.
One extra note: If you're signed up for one of Google's AI plans at the $20-per-month tier or higher, you get Google Health Premium thrown in as part of it (as well as Google Home Premium and YouTube Premium Lite).
It's possible that you want all the Google Health Premium extras but find the AI Coach a bit intrusive. It does take a very proactive stance when it comes to giving you tips and pointers, but it can be a bit too eager to help.
To hide it from view, tap your profile picture (top right), then Google Health settings > Coach . From here you can opt out of the Coach feature entirely or just hide the main insights from view. (You'll still be able to ask questions about your data.) When you need the coach’s encouragement and you want to turn it back on, you can do so in the same place.

Kindles are getting costlier faster than they’re getting better.
Supply pressures, shortages, and inflation have pushed tech prices relentlessly upward over the last half-decade, and even basic gadgets haven’t been immune. That’s why you can spend $385 on a Raspberry Pi, or why the cheapest Amazon Kindle in 2026 costs more than the midrange one from a few years ago . “New thing, better features, same price” used to be a reliable formula, but now you’re lucky if you can get the same thing for barely more than before.
The 2024 Kindles all came with small price increases, but the 2026 models make them look like stellar deals. The $160 Kindle Paperwhite from two years ago wipes the floor with this year’s $150 Kindle in just about every conceivable way, from screen size to front light quality to waterproofing—something to consider if you’re choosing between a used or refurbished Paperwhite and one of these new models.
The flagship of the now five-model-large monochrome Kindle family is the $250 2026 Paperwhite Signature Edition, which takes the core specs of the new $200 Paperwhite and puts it in a sturdy iPad-esque aluminum case instead of the typical plastic.
It’s an exceptionally nice reader, and if you’re down with paying even more for it, longtime page-turn button holdouts can recover their precious buttons while still getting the benefits of new, fast Kindle hardware. With the exception of one regression—wireless charging, a feature of the 2024 Signature Edition that has been removed here—it’s the fastest and nicest Kindle you can get. It’s mostly the value, or lack thereof, that leaves a bad taste in one’s mouth.
Unlike the 2021 or 2024 Kindle Paperwhite updates, the 2026 Paperwhite doesn’t include any notable screen or lighting upgrades. Anyone upgrading from a two- or three-generation-old version of the hardware will still get an upgrade, but the 2026 Paperwhite isn’t doing a ton to push the category forward. And while speed increases were front-and-center in Amazon’s promotional material for the 2024 Paperwhite, Amazon isn’t highlighting any particular gains for this year’s Paperwhite (the base Kindle does apparently open books 30 percent faster than the previous-generation Kindle, though).
But the Paperwhite and this year’s basic Kindle both make a couple of tweaks worth mentioning that don’t really show up on a spec sheet. One is that the device’s power button moves from the bottom edge to the top-right edge, a small change I appreciate because I’ve accidentally pressed the bottom-mounted power button all the times I’ve tried to set the Kindle on the edge of something. The other is that the devices now have user-replaceable batteries, a change made in part to comply with right-to-repair regulations going into effect in some countries.
Whether you’re buying the standard plastic-backed Paperwhite or the aluminum Signature Edition, you’re still getting a 7-inch 300 PPI screen with a front light that can adjust its color temperature as well as its brightness, which I find makes the Paperwhite easier on the eyes than the harsher, more bluish-tinted front light on older Kindles and the basic 2026 Kindle. The plastic Paperwhite is a smidge lighter than the 2024 version, and the Signature Edition is a little heavier (thanks in part to the aluminum casing), though not by a lot in either direction.
Whether it’s faster than the 2024 Paperwhite or not, the snappy and fluid performance I observed while using that device is definitely present in this one. The E-Ink screen still puts a cap on exactly how fluid and responsive the device can feel, but you rarely feel the big gap between your touch input and the device responding to that input like you can on most older Kindles. (I tried repeatedly to run the old Google Octane 2.0 benchmark I used to get a sense of the 2024 Paperwhite’s relative performance, but it could never complete a run in either the 2026 Kindle or the 2026 Paperwhite’s browser, for whatever reason).
I didn’t spend as much time with it, but I did test the basic 6-inch Kindle alongside the Paperwhite Signature Edition.
Overall, I like the updated look and feel of the redesigned Kindle, particularly the fact that the screen and bezel are now flush, as the last few Paperwhites have been. And despite using the same 6-inch screen size as older Paperwhites, Amazon has significantly shrunk the overall size and weight of the device. It doesn’t quite look like a “Kindle mini” next to the current Paperwhite, but it’s not far off.
But you’re still getting less for your money than you were a few years ago. If you compare the 2026 Kindle to the 2024 or 2022 model, and you ignore what each one of those devices cost to buy, it looks like slow and steady improvement. But the fact is that you can pay $150 for this Kindle and lose important features, like the warm light and waterproofing, that Amazon offered in the 2021 Paperwhite for just $140 back in 2021.
That’s just the reality of buying technology right now. “Get more for the same money” is out. Now if you want more, you have to pay more.
The new Paperwhite Signature Edition’s biggest upgrade, should you choose to pay for it, is the addition of page-turn buttons. Page-turn buttons by proxy, at least.
The Signature Edition adds iPad-style copper contacts on the back, and for another $80 (on top of the $250 you’ll pay for the Kindle) you can buy a Kindle Page Turn Cover in various colors that connects to those contacts with pogo pins. It’s the cover that adds the buttons. Amazon also offers a $60 charging stand that uses the pins, the closest equivalent for the now-removed wireless charging feature.
The cover really does make the new Paperwhite look and feel a bit more like a Frankenstein Kindle Oasis, right down to the asymmetrical edge that the button area adds. And the page-turn buttons themselves feel good and work well. The physical feedback from clicky buttons and the Kindle’s overall responsiveness both make page turns feel nearly instantaneous when you press it to turn a single page. Clicking the buttons quickly to turn multiple pages still gets bogged down a little.
Functionally, the worst things I can say about the Page Turn Cover are that it adds to the reader’s size and weight, and the power button doesn’t feel nearly as good as the page-turn buttons. The case’s “button” is basically a little plastic nub that pushes in the device’s actual built-in power button. At least with the hardware I bought, the case’s button feels like it can’t consistently reach the device button, which means it wasn’t always reliable. This is partly moot because opening and closing the cover also wakes and sleeps the device.
Amazon offers one cheaper option for every other Kindle that can run the newest version of the Kindle operating system: a $35 remote control-style Kindle Click . As a completely separate accessory you have to hold or rest on something in order to use, I don’t find this to be a particularly compelling solution to the “no buttons” problem. But it’s also the only version of “clickable buttons” that Amazon offers for less than $330. It is what it is.
The Kindle Click requires a Kindle running version 5.20.1.0.2 or later of the Kindle operating system. Currently, that version only runs on the 2024 and 2026 Kindles, plus 2022’s Kindle Scribe. It seems as though Amazon has gotten stingier with long-tail Kindle OS updates than it was in 2024, when all Kindles going back to 2018 could run the same software. The 2018 Kindles currently top out at 5.18, while the other 2021/22 Kindles stop at 5.19.
The last reader Amazon offered with page-turn buttons was 2019’s $249 Kindle Oasis, which was dinged pretty much across the board for being “expensive.” Today’s Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition will cost you just as much, but charge you $80 extra for the case and buttons. It’s a nicer reader in some important ways, most notably its USB-C port and much-improved performance. But that’s still a pretty substantia…

NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has concluded its scientific mission , which spanned just under 22 years. As its orbital altitude fell below 275 kilometers (171 miles), it could no longer continue stable astronomical observations, and it reentered the atmosphere on November 4 over North Sumatra, Indonesia.
Swift had been launched on November 20, 2004, as the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer, and it began operations the following month. In addition to a gamma-ray-burst alert telescope, it was equipped with ultraviolet and visible-light telescopes as well as an x-ray telescope, and was designed as a multi-wavelength observation satellite capable of rapidly pinpointing the locations of gamma-ray bursts—the most powerful explosions in the universe. In 2018, following the death of its first principal investigator, Neil Gehrels, NASA renamed the mission in his honor.
The development of the Swift space telescope was driven by the difficulty of tracking gamma-ray bursts. “Swift was designed as a satellite dedicated to studying gamma-ray bursts, outbursts that came and went so quickly that no one could target them with large telescopes to learn more,” explains S. Bradley Cenko, the mission’s principal investigator at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center.
Swift detected a gamma-ray burst, pinpointed its location, relayed the information to other observatories, and then swiveled its telescope to capture images before the afterglow faded; this sequence of operations was usually finished in about a minute. Speed was particularly critical for short gamma-ray bursts, in which the emissions end in less than two seconds. Before Swift was launched, it was not possible to pinpoint the location quickly and accurately enough to observe the afterglow.
In May 2005, Swift quickly turned toward the gamma-ray burst GRB 050509B, which lasted only 0.03 second, and detected 11 x-ray photons. This was the first short gamma-ray burst for which an afterglow was detected. This observation corroborated long-standing theoretical models suggesting that short bursts are most likely caused by the merger of two neutron stars, celestial bodies with a mass comparable to the sun compressed to the size of a city.
Its flexible observation planning system is another reason why Swift was regarded as a versatile tool for astronomy. This is because astronomers could request target-of-opportunity observations, which allowed commands to be sent from the ground in as little as a few minutes.
It also allowed for the setup of monitoring programs to observe specific celestial objects for periods ranging from minutes to months, and it was possible to schedule observations of up to 75 distinct celestial objects per day. Furthermore, it played a role in sending alerts to other space- and ground-based facilities to coordinate additional observations.
Swift observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and more than 1,400 supernova explosions. It also witnessed stars being torn apart by black holes, monitored active galaxies, and conducted all-sky x-ray surveys; the data from these observations contributed to approximately 7,000 scientific papers. The entire dataset—including approximately 22 years’ worth of brightness measurements and more than 1.5 million images from ultraviolet and visible-light telescopes— is publicly available and amounts to about 12 terabytes.
The Swift observatory was circling in low Earth orbit. At this altitude even the outermost layer of the atmosphere creates air resistance on satellites. However, Swift lacked thrusters to maintain its orbit, and its altitude continued to drop.
As a result, its altitude—which was approximately 585 kilometers (364 miles) at launch—had dropped to about 363 kilometers as of June 18, 2026. In recent years, increased solar activity has caused Earth’s atmosphere to expand, causing the telescope to descend faster than initially predicted.
NASA engineers had long predicted that Swift’s altitude would drop to approximately 300 kilometers by the fall of 2026, at which point a recovery spacecraft would no longer be able to approach it safely. Consequently, NASA decided not to issue a standard request for proposals and instead asked three companies with which it had already signed technology development contracts to explore the feasibility of providing orbital services. In September 2025, NASA signed a $30 million contract with the space startup Katalyst Space Technologies.
The Swift Space Telescope upon its completion in September 2003. Pictured alongside it is Neil Gehrels, the project’s first principal investigator. (NASA)
The original plan was for the small satellite LINK to capture and dock with Swift using three robotic arms, raise its orbit to a safe operational altitude, and resume scientific observations. Since there was only one year to complete this task, Katalyst manufactured components in-house when suppliers could not meet their deadlines and streamlined testing procedures. LINK was launched on July 3, 2026, aboard a Northrop Grumman Pegasus XL rocket.
However, during in-orbit testing, a malfunction occurred in LINK’s attitude-control system, and it was determined that capturing Swift and raising its orbit would be difficult. In response, NASA and Katalyst announced on August 19 that the operation would be canceled, and the mission was redefined as an in-orbit demonstration.
LINK raised its orbit to align with Swift, deployed its three robotic arms, and simultaneously fired its three ion thrusters, successfully approaching the telescope to a distance of 12 to 15 kilometers (7 to 9 miles). Nevertheless, NASA announced that LINK would not approach Swift any closer during the remainder of its operational life in orbit. LINK subsequently reentered Earth’s atmosphere on September 25.
Following the decision to abandon the orbital raise, the Swift operations team announced a plan to continue observations for as long as possible in the time left. On August 26, they restarted the ultraviolet- and visible-light telescopes and the x-ray telescope—which had been shut down in preparation for the rescue mission—and successfully captured images of Tycho’s supernova remnant, located approximately 13,000 light-years away. But as the altitude dropped below 275 kilometers, the telescope was no longer able to maintain a stable lock on its target, and the scientific mission concluded with the final observation on October 20.
“Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long,” said Sean Domagall-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA headquarters. To ensure it can continue to respond swiftly to cosmic phenomena even after Swift is gone, NASA is considering ways to utilize and expand its existing fleet of space telescopes.

Dark matter accounts for approximately 85 percent of all matter in the universe, though that’s about all we really know about the mysterious substance. Scientists believe it because of the gravitational effects it has on galaxies and other cosmic structures , but since it doesn’t otherwise interact with ordinary matter, it’s been a challenge for scientists to determine what it’s really made of.
For decades, scientists have been trying to determine whether dark matter consists of a single type of particle or if it’s made up of several particles that could have different properties and thus different interactions with the surrounding world. Earlier this year, scientists found the most convincing evidence of a dark matter particle yet, and if the second scenario is true, it’s possible we could find more.
This second possibility also raises an intriguing question: If there are a variety of “dark particles,” could they interact and combine with one another—just as the particles we know do —to form their own dark atoms and molecules? If that were the case, the dark universe could be much more complex than researchers had initially imagined.
But luckily, humanity has already faced a similar challenge in trying to understand the diversity of ordinary matter. Though to many introductory chemistry students, the periodic table can seem like an odd way to organize information, it’s one of the most ingenious tools developed in our understanding of the physical world. This classification system doesn’t just order the elements, but reveals patterns among their properties that even helped predict the existence of other elements that had not yet been discovered.
Now, a team of five physicists is exploring a scenario in which dark matter could form different classes of nuclei and atoms, governed by their own rules . Their research suggests that we may need something similar to a periodic table to understand the organization of dark matter.
The hypothesis at the heart of this research seems straight out of science fiction . The researchers propose that our universe would contain a kind of “ mirror sector ,” where particles that barely interact with visible matter have their own forces and can interact with one another.
The idea is not new and is quite serious. The “Mirror Twin Higgs” was proposed two decades ago as a possible solution to a problem related to the mass of the Higgs boson . According to this theory, mirror particles would help offset certain quantum effects that might otherwise cause its mass to be much greater than what we observe . Although the existence of these particles has never been proven, the proposal offered an ingenious way to address the problem without requiring all new particles to be visible to detectors .
One of the creators of the Mirror Twin Higgs theory, physicist Zackaria Chacko, is part of this new investigation that extends this hypothesis into the dark matter puzzle. Along with several collaborators, he explores in this recent preprint what would happen if particles from this hypothetical mirror sector could combine with one another, forming nuclei, atoms, and a variety of dark elements.
Their calculations suggest that, under certain conditions, these particles could combine to form dark equivalents of some of the elements we know, ranging from the simplest to others as complex as carbon. However, this would not be an exact copy of our matter . The dark particles would have different masses and properties, which would also change the rules governing how they bond, what structures they can form , and which ones remain stable.
For example, in the researchers’ model, dark hydrogen atoms would be unstable and could not survive as those in our universe do. This is a striking difference when we consider that hydrogen is the simplest and most abundant element in ordinary matter.
If these dark elements were ever discovered, understanding the rules governing their formation would be essential for classifying them. A sort of “dark periodic table” could help bring order to that diversity, just as it did with the elements we know.
For now, this all remains in the realm of theoretical physics . Researchers have not observed any of these atoms, and some doubt such structures could actually form. But there’s plenty about dark matter we have yet to discover.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Diyarbakır Barosu eski Başkanı Tahir Elçi'nin öldürülmesinin üzerinden 11 yıl geçti. Davada hiçbir sanık ceza almadı ve pek çok karanlık nokta aydınlatılmadı.
Avukat Tahir Elçi, Diyarbakır Barosu Başkanı iken 28 Kasım 2015 tarihinde yaptığı bir basın açıklaması sırasında başından vurularak öldürüldü. 11 yıl önce Diyarbakır'ın Sur ilçesinde, kentin sembollerinden Dört Ayaklı Minare önünde güvenlik güçleri ile PKK'lılar arasında çıkan silahlı çatışma sırasında öldürülen Tahir Elçi, faili meçhul dosyaların aydınlatılması için verdiği hukuk mücadelesiyle biliniyordu.
Ancak Elçi'nin öldürülmesi de şu an için "faili meçhul" olarak kaldı . Elçi'nin öldürülmesine ilişkin davada karar 12 Haziran 2024'te çıktı. Diyarbakır 10. Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi'nde görülen davada, biri ihraç edilmiş üç polisin tutuksuz, cinayetin yaşandığı sokağa ateş ederek giren PKK'lı Uğur Yakışır'ın ise firari olarak yargılandığı davada polisler beraat etti . "İki polisi öldürme" ve "ülke birliğini ve bütünlüğünü bozmak" suçlarından üç kez ağırlaştırılmış müebbet ve 45 yıl hapis cezasıyla yargılanan Yakışır'ın dosyası ise Elçi cinayeti davasından ayrılmıştı.
Sanıklar hakkında beraat kararı verilmesinin ardından Elçi ailesinin avukatları Ocak 2025'te istinaf başvurusu yaptı ancak Diyarbakır Bölge Adliye Mahkemesi 10. Ceza Dairesi, istinaf başvurusunu esastan reddetti. Bunun üzerine dava Anayasa Mahkemesi'ne (AYM) taşındı. Dosyanın AYM'deki incelemesi devam ediyor.
Cinayete ilişkin iddianame dört buçuk yılda hazırlandı. Uzun süre sürüncemede bırakılan soruşturma dosyası Diyarbakır Barosu'nun Londra Üniversitesi Adli Mimarlık Bölümü'ne hazırlattığı raporun ardından tamamlandı.
Raporda olağan şüpheli olarak gösterilen üç polis ve ateş ederek sokağa giren Uğur Yakışır hakkında dava açıldı. İddianamede, sanıkların hangisinin Elçi'nin ölümünden sorumlu olduğunun tespitinin imkânsız, ancak her üç polisin de kuvvetli suç şüphesi altında olduğu ifade edildi. İddianameyi kabul eden Diyarbakır 10'uncu Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi davanın başka şehre nakledilmesini istedi ama Adalet Bakanlığı bu talebi reddetti.
Raporda, Elçi'nin hayatını kaybetmesine neden olan kurşunun üç polisten birinin silahından çıktığı tespiti yer aldı. Diyarbakır Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı, üç polis hakkında kovuşturma başlattı.
20 Mart 2020'de tamamlanan iddianamede, polisler M. S., F. T. ve S. T. hakkında "bilinçli taksirle ölüme neden olmak" suçundan 3 yıldan 9 yıla kadar hapis cezası talep edildi. Dava ise 21 Ekim 2020'de başladı.
Elçi ailesinin avukatları, etkili soruşturma yürütülmediğini ve delillerin toplanmadığını belirterek pek çok kez soruşturma sürecindeki eksikliklere dikkat çekti. Diyarbakır Barosu'nda soruşturmayı takip etmek için kurulan komisyonda görev yapan Avukat Gamze Yalçın, 83 parça delilin çoğunun toplanamadığın ifade etti. Elçi'nin ölümüne neden olan merminin çekirdeği de bulunamadı .
Cinayetin karanlıkta kalan noktalarından biri kamera görüntüleriydi. Onlarca kamera olmasına rağmen vurulma anının görüntüsü bulunamadı. Ayrıca polis kamerası kaydında Elçi'nin vurulma anına denk gelen 13 saniye, PTT güvenlik kamerasında da 17 dakika kesinti yapıldığı tespit edildi. Dosyadaki belgeyi inceleyen avukatlar, ardışık şekilde numaralandırılan görüntülerin bir kısmının silindiğini belirledi.
Soruşturma sürecinde Elçi'nin vurulduğu Yıkıkkaya Sokak'ta bulunan Mardin Kebap Evi isimli işyerinin güvenlik kamerası kayıtlarına el konulmuştu. Yapılan incelemede dükkânın içini gösteren üç kameranın çalıştığı tespit edilirken Elçi'nin vurulduğu sokağı gören dördüncü kamera ise açılamadı.
23 Haziran 2017 tarihinde tamamlanan ve soruşturma sürecinde avukatların sürekli dosyaya getirilmesini istedikleri, mülkiye ve polis müfettişlerinin hazırladığı rapor dosyaya 2022'de girdi . Raporda, Elçi cinayetinin önceden tasarlanmış bir eylem olmadığı ifade edildi.
Mahkeme ara kararını 5 Temmuz 2023'te açıkladı. Elçi ailesinin; olay yerinde keşif yapılması, mülkiye ve polis başmüfettişleri ile polislerin yanı sıra olay yerindeki Güvenlik Şube Amiri ve dönemin başbakanı olan Gelecek Partisi Genel Başkanı Ahmet Davutoğlu'nun tanık olarak dinlenmesi yönündeki taleplerinin tümü reddedildi.
Savcı, 29 Nisan 2024'teki duruşmada esas hakkındaki mütalaasını sundu. Savcılık, Tahir Elçi'nin ölümüne sebep olan kurşunun, hangi silahtan çıktığının belirlenmesinin, "tıbben ve fiziken mümkün olmadığı" yönünde görüş vererek üç polisin de beraat etmesini istedi.
Mütalaada, "Sonuç olarak sanık polislerin maktule yönelik olarak bilinçli taksirle ölüme neden olma suçunu işlediklerine dair mahkumiyetlerine yeterli her türlü şüpheden uzak, kesin ve inandırıcı delil elde edilememesi karşısında (...) suçun sanıklar tarafından işlendiğinin sabit olmaması nedeniyle beraatine karar verilmesi kamu adına talep ve mütalaa olunur" ifadeleri yer aldı.
Diyarbakır 10'uncu Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi, 12 Haziran 2024'te verdiği kararla, "sanıkların üzerine atılı suçu işlediğine dair her türlü şüpheden uzak delil bulunmadığı" gerekçesiyle sanıkların beraatine karar verdi.
1966 yılında Şırnak'ın Cizre ilçesinde doğan Tahir Elçi, ilk ve ortaokul öğrenimlerini burada tamamladı. 1991'de İstanbul Üniversitesi Hukuk Fakültesi'nden mezun olan Elçi, avukatlığa 1992'de Diyarbakır'da başladı.
1990'lı yıllarda Kürtlerin yoğun olarak yaşadığı şehirlerdeki insan hakları ihlallerine ve faili meçhul cinayetlere karşı mağdur ailelerin hukuk mücadelesine destek veren Elçi, 1998-2006 yılları arasında Diyarbakır Barosu yönetiminde çeşitli görevlerde bulundu.
Türkiye İnsan Hakları Vakfı'nın (TİHV) kurucularından olan Tahir Elçi, İnsan Hakları Derneği (İHD) ve Türkiye Barolar Birliği'nde (TBB) de çeşitli görevler üstlendi. 2012'de Diyarbakır Barosu Başkanı olan Elçi, 2014'te aynı göreve tekrar seçildi .
Öldürüldüğü sırada Diyarbakır Barosu Başkanı olan Tahir Elçi, o dönem şiddetlenen çatışmalara karşı 28 Kasım 2015 tarihinde Diyarbakır'ın Sur ilçesinde tarihi Dört Ayaklı Minare'nin önünde bir basın açıklaması düzenliyordu. Çatışmalara son verilmesi gerektiğini belirten Elçi'nin son sözleri, "Silah, çatışma, operasyon istemiyoruz" oldu.
Tahir Elçi, ölümünden kısa süre önce bir televizyon programında kullandığı ifadeler nedeniyle hedef gösterilmişti. Elçi, 15 Ekim 2015 tarihinde CNN Türk'te yayınlanan bir televizyon programında "PKK terör örgütü değildir. Bazı eylemleri terör niteliğinde olsa bile PKK, silahlı siyasal bir harekettir. Siyasal talepleri olan, çok ciddi bir desteği olan bir siyasal harekettir" dediği için "terör örgütü propagandası yapmak" suçlamasıyla gözaltına alınmış, daha sonra adli kontrol şartıyla serbest bırakılmıştı.
Bu sözleri nedeniyle tehdit edilen Elçi hakkında ölümünden kısa süre önce 1,5 yıldan 7,5 yıla kadar hapis cezası istemiyle iddianame hazırlanmıştı.

Meta claims its Muse assistant will make users’ lives easier, but business owners say AI is driving them to go analogue
R estaurant owners are battling a horde of AI bots and returning to using the telephone instead of online booking as new virtual assistants launch in the UK – but sometimes even that isn’t enough to stop them.
This week, Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta launched its Muse AI assistant in the UK and is encouraging users to let it shop and make restaurant reservations. The bot is given access to the user’s email if they give it permission, and it can make restaurant bookings and go shopping on the user’s behalf.
Muse has been downloaded millions of times in the US, but it has caused chaos for restaurants. The online booking platform Resy has banned bots after restaurants on the platform were swarmed with agents that can refresh the page thousands of times and snap up all the reservations. Now, AI agents are plaguing venues in the UK.
Dave Strauss, the co-owner of Bouchon Racine, which was recently crowned UK restaurant of the year , said he had already had an argument with a would-be diner’s AI bot.
He answers the phones in his French restaurant every day from 11am to take reservation requests and said recently he received an unnerving call: “The other day I answered the phone to an AI bot that sounded very realistic. There was something a bit wrong about it – it sounded exactly like a human being, but something was off. I asked if it was a bot and it said: ‘Yes this is an AI booking process.’”
Strauss added: “I had an argument with the AI bot and told it to never call me again. But that wasn’t very satisfying as it didn’t argue back.”
Kimberley Coke, a high-end restaurant concierge, is paid by celebrities to secure a good table at top dining spots. She said she was worried about the swarm of AI bots: “I think it is terrifying and it could cause absolute chaos.”
Coke, who makes all her bookings via WhatsApp or phone calls, added: “There is now so much information you can get online about the hottest restaurants and where to go, and it is really hard to get the tables and that is why people come to me as I have personal relationships with the restaurants. With the apps, you don’t know who the client is, you have no background on who is coming in, they still might not show up. There is nothing worse for a restaurant in December when they have empty tables.”
Meta has claimed that its product can make people’s lives easier, but that has not been the case for the restaurants on the receiving end of the calls, emails and reservation app bookings.
The problem has been pronounced in New York City, where hard-to-secure restaurant tables are a status symbol. One of the most popular is 4 Charles Prime Rib, which serves a famous double wagyu cheeseburger, often served topped with a fried egg. It has been a popular target for AI agents, with sources at Resy saying they were having to ban multiple accounts using bots to book reservations there.
Strauss said: “There has been a constant shift to make everything as automated as possible to save a bit of money. We believe here that doesn’t work. We get a lot of emails now saying we can outsource our bookings and phone calls to AI. That makes us more keen on doing it the way that we do it. If I could get rid of online booking, I would.”
Jeremy King, who owns Simpson’s in the Strand , Arlington and the Park, said that the move towards depersonalising interactions by using AI was making him go “more analogue” in his restaurants – diners will find it much easier to snag a prime table at one of his venues by picking up the phone.
He said: “I am very happy to embrace new technology but ultimately if it conspires against us we will have to return to managing without.”
Such agents are likely to become more common in the UK and Meta has deals with an array of British businesses – including Marks & Spencer, Currys, Sainsbury’s and easyJet – allowing Muse to navigate their websites more easily and to access their apps. If a company does not offer a “connector” app that Muse can visit, the agent will access its website instead.
The Information Commissioner’s Office and the Competition and Markets Authority said they had been in talks with Meta before Muse’s launch about its responsibility to comply with UK laws. The ICO, the UK’s data protection watchdog, said on Tuesday the tech company had committed to a “voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme”, while the CMA said talks had resulted in changes to make the app’s terms and conditions fairer

As Anthropic cashes in on the stock market, human-made masterpieces need greater defence from endless extraction
Grand Theft Auto VI came out on the same day that Anthropic made its stock market debut. I keep thinking about that coincidence. As more than one tech writer has pointed out, the new GTA took 13 years to make, more than $1bn of investment and involved 9,000 sets of human hands, and it will probably be the last blockbuster video game to be fully free of generative AI.
On the day of its release, a group chat with my most gaming-minded male friends erupted in discussion about whether or not video games, and GTA VI specifically, rose to the level of art. Exploring a national park? Yes, that’s there . Badly assemble a coffee table from “Krapea” (the game’s fictional furniture company)? Ditto. Eating a hot dog? Why not. All of it gloriously human in origin. Perhaps that in itself is an argument for how GTA VI crosses the blurry line from entertainment to something more. It is a medium by which human beings offer others a (necessarily incomplete) interpretation of what it’s like to be them in the world, or to try to transcend it.
At the very least, Grand Theft Auto is a franchise that has always offered at least a glimmer of social critique – even in its early 2000s iterations – amid its otherwise overwhelming scope for virtual hedonism and violence. Olivier Mauco, a French political scientist and author of GTA IV: the Flipside of the American Dream, sees that 2008 version of the game as a turning point : away from pure provocation and towards an acerbic dissection of US aspiration, which remains out of reach for the game’s immigrant protagonist, who has fled war in the Balkans and remains forever marginalised.
In this latest version, Jason and Lucia experience the same “ desperation capitalism ” that might induce you to try to trade your way out of a broken, oligarchic economy – or just want to burn the system down. At the same time, there is no shortage of laments from far-right gamer bros who find the storyline and gameplay too “woke”, because it nudges players towards an empathetic and balanced romantic partnership, rather than a misogynistic one – even while also allowing you to run over elderly people with their own mobility scooters just for the hell of it.
As Wired points out , GTA VI “is bristling with parodies of toxic manosphere content and crypto scams. Random characters on the street will spout Maga-coded conspiracy theories and call you a ‘libtard’ or ‘commie socialist’ if you walk into them … Yet the provocation of asking guys to consider acts of service for a virtual girlfriend could prove the most revolutionary element.”
Whether Rockstar Games , the company behind the GTA franchise, timed it on purpose or not, it feels pertinent that on the same day that tens of millions were entering an all-encompassing virtual space where cars, bicycles, airplanes and boats are there for the taking, the most lucrative grand cultural theft in human history was playing out in the markets. Generative AI would be impossible without having vacuumed up almost the sum total of human creative output. All of our words, music, paintings; our attempts to deal with the emotional experience of the world, have been “acquired” and handed to an algorithm incapable of either emotion or experience.
Journalism is one victim of AI “scraping” cannibalising the providers of expensive-to-produce reporting. Here in France, where Google’s AI Overview was legally blocked until July, the impact on newspapers has been devastating and swift : for Libération, a decline in site visits of more than 30%, and nearly 20% for Le Monde.
Stories abound from writers whose books were pirated by Anthropic and others, and to whom Anthropic offered an insultingly low settlement : a mere 0.1% of the company’s valuation at its IPO, or roughly $3,000 (£2,300) per pirated work (of which publishers will then take half). Even to acquire that paltry $1,500, many writers have spent months jumping through bureaucratic hoops trying to get paid. Meanwhile, Anthropic’s seven co-founders have hauled in paper fortunes worth $180bn, and even an average employee could now be worth more than $40m.
In the real world, the world of Grand Theft Anthropic , nobody is coming to save us. The courts have too often abdicated the spirit of the law meant to protect creative works. Governments have ceded common sense to an oligarchic billionaire class, and the avaricious logic that always demands more, when it comes to data centres and compute.
Last week, I had a video call with Gabriel and Isaque, the Brazilian co-developers of a piece of software called ShieldFont , an open-source project hoping to protect content written by humans by “poisoning” unauthorised AI training. ShieldFont uses a dictionary of nearly 12,000 words that it scrambles when they are detected in writing, in such a way that the result seems grammatically and semantically legible, all while actually being nonsense. When the text is rendered visually, we read the correct version, while an AI scraping webpage ingests the “poisoned” text, which corrupts its dataset.
The pair originally created ShieldFont to protect their own website, but then realised that by making it open-source (meaning, for example, that media organisations could keep their own custom typefaces and still implement ShieldFont), it could potentially become a meaningful deterrent against non-consensual scraping. “I was thinking of the song Toxicity by System of a Down, and the line that goes ‘How do you own disorder?’,” Gabriel told me. “Of course, you can’t own disorder, and so the idea was to use chaos as a tool against chaos.”
The pair stressed to me that their intent is to fight unauthorised AI scraping, not AI as a whole. But considering how much unauthorised and unethical scraping already underlies the trillion-dollar AI industry, I can’t help but have a more mischievous, more GTA-worthy thought. Taken as a whole, news organisations (including this one) and Wikipedia are sitting on billions of lines of text. If these sites were wholesale converted to ShieldFont and then scraped, it would be a first shot fired at poisoning the data well of generative AI.
Like in Grand Theft Auto, these companies and their billionaires have hijacked the car and they’re taking us for a ride. In life, as in the game, chaos abounds. But in Grand Theft Anthropic, we are not NPCs: non-player characters. So maybe it’s time to grab the wheel.

Corsair is known primarily for its high-end gaming peripherals and accessories, as well as PC components like memory and power supplies. More recently, the company even dipped its toe into full-on, prebuilt gaming PCs . So, if you’re shopping for a new gaming keyboard or building a new PC , checking out Corsair’s website is a good way to go. But before you buy, we have some Corsair discount codes and Corsair coupons to help you save some extra cash.
We all know that it’s never been more expensive to build or upgrade a PC. The memory shortage has taken its toll, graphics cards are in demand, and wide-ranging economic uncertainty has led to a situation where upgrading your PC or building one from scratch is outrageously expensive. Corsair is offering up to 30% off its most popular gaming products, which include components like memory, PC cases, and power supplies.
This also includes gaming-related peripherals, such as one of our favorite gaming headsets, the Corsair Void V2 Wireless . WIRED reviewer Brad Bourque found this model to be a particularly good fit for people with larger heads, while remaining lightweight and comfortable with its breathable earcups.
Like many companies, Corsair offers a 15% discount for students, which is always helpful for saving some extra money. It does, however, require a valid student email address and a UNiDAYS account. Once you’re signed up, though, you’re on your way to 15% off Corsair’s entire catalog.
For college students looking to do some gaming on the weekends, I’d recommend checking out one of the company’s gaming mice, such as the Corsair Sabre V2 Carbon Fiber and Magnesium Gaming Mouse . This pro-level esports mouse, which our mouse reviewer gave a very high 9/10 score, praising its extremely light design and comfortable shape. At the time of publication, it was 30% off, bringing the price down to $120.
One of the best ways to save on pricey gaming gear like processors, memory storage, monitors, and more, is to check out Corsair’s online deals special offers page . Here, they have deals on a myriad of best-selling tech, including gaming PCs, monitors, gaming deals, memory deals, and discounts on Revival Series items (their refurbished like-new tech line). Right now, some of the best deals are a VENGEANCE a7500 Gaming PC for $3,300—a $500 discount, and the best-selling VIRTUOSO RGB WIRELESS High-Fidelity Gaming Headset for only $90.
Unlike a lot of tech manufacturers, Corsair actually sells its own refurbished products that have been certified by the company itself. Products are up to 50% off the full retail price, and I saw some solid deals while perusing, including on its popular K90 and K70 series of keyboards, which we recently reviewed .
The selection of refurbished products is extensive, including lots of different PC components. That includes CPU coolers, case fans, and power supplies—as well as entire prebuilt gaming PCs.
There’s one more way to save some extra money when shopping with Corsair. The company has a text alert discount code that you can sign up for. If you sign up for text alerts, you’ll also get a 10% Corsair discount code that can be applied to your shopping cart. Every little bit helps, especially if you’re putting together an entire PC with Corsair components.
Buying a like-new tech product is a great way to make a small investment with a big payoff. Rather than drop thousands on a brand-new gadget, snag a like-new refurbished item at Corsair. If you’re looking to upgrade your gaming setup or WFH haven for way less, be sure to check out Corsair’s refurbished products page. There you’ll find deeply discounted gaming PCs, LCD touchscreens, and more.

Experts suggest AI companies may be sitting on ‘bombshell’ that could have severe consequences for secret information
Leading experts and the governor of the Bank of England have suggested that top AI companies might have something under their hat – a “bombshell” revelation about encryption. Depending on what it is, it could have major consequences for the world’s secret information, and the banks and governments that hold and transmit it.
This is because of recent, startling mathematical advances made by AI models, which are still being understood.
Leading computer scientists think that artificial intelligence companies may have recently made a discovery related to cryptography, the mathematics behind how the world encodes secret information. There are different possibilities for what this discovery could be.
Whatever it is, it could have big ramifications for secret information held by banks, governments and intelligence agencies. Either they might shortly find out that there is a way for adversaries and hackers to break into their information, or they might find out that this information is more secure than they thought.
Before this, it was widely thought that quantum computers, once developed, would allow the decoding of the world’s encrypted information. Governments and tech companies had started to prepare for “Q-Day”, the day when quantum computers would be able to break modern cryptography. But that potential event was considered to be years, if not decades, away.
Now, depending on what has been discovered, such a revelation – and, potentially, chaos – could come in weeks or months.
There have been significant mathematical breakthroughs in recent weeks. These include proof of the Riemann hypothesis by the mathematician Levent Alpöge, working in concert with the AI model Claude.
These proofs have not been fully verified by humans, but they have been verified by a rigorous coding language called Lean, so mathematicians think they are likely to be substantive.
Some of the problems that have been solved relate to cryptography. Some are significant and have been the subject of entire careers.
Leading computer scientists think that, if AI has broken ground on these problems, it is overwhelmingly likely it has, or will soon, produce revelations about the core mathematics behind encoding the world’s information.
Scott Aaronson, a preeminent computer scientist, cited a recent proof – from Anthropic and OpenAI – that VP≠VNP, a finding that he says has led him to drink uncharacteristic amounts of wine in his kitchen.
In basic terms, this proof is about what problems can be solved easily by the computers we have, and what problems are truly “hard” problems – meaning that the world’s most powerful computers could not solve them in, say, a lifetime.
Theoretical computer scientists are interested in this question: are all problems in the world quickly solvable with good enough algorithms, or are there problems that might take vast amounts of time to solve, and for which no shortcuts are possible?
Anthropic and OpenAI’s proof that VP≠VNP is a major step forward in answering this question, which was first posed in the 1970s. While it concerns a slightly different problem from breaking encryption, it suggests that AI models can work ably in this territory and produce groundbreaking results.
The world was abuzz over the summer with claims new, powerful AI models – such as Mythos – were capable of finding hundreds of vulnerabilities in lines of code.
Put one way, this amounts to finding lots of grammatical errors in the language of computers. It isn’t particularly difficult, but artificial intelligence can do it well. AI can also help cyber-attackers find these errors and exploit them.
Breaking encryption is a far more fundamental challenge. It means making a novel mathematical discovery, which stands to illuminate our conceptual understanding of how computers work.
Encryption is based on the idea that some maths problems are too “hard” for computers to break, no matter how many GPUs you shove into a datacentre. But this is a very abstract thing to argue.
Governments, banks and tech companies have been updating the encryption they use in anticipation of powerful quantum computers coming online. Their new methods – or old methods – may be resilient to decryption algorithms.
If they were not resilient, and a decryption algorithm were discovered, that algorithm could still be difficult to implement in practice.
Still, the extreme scenario is vast amounts of information, from Swift bank transfers to the private messages of government officials could suddenly be read by those who could access it. This could include secure exchanges from decades ago.
Many intelligence agencies put listening devices on cables to collect information transmitted through them. One example is GCHQ. Such agencies may not have been able to crack this information up to now, but that could suddenly change.

Exclusive: AI may have cracked decades-old maths problems that underpin encryption at banks and government agencies
AI companies are sitting on “bombshell” revelations that could disrupt a cornerstone of security for banks and governments in as soon as a few months, leading experts believe.
Scott Aaronson, a pre-eminent theoretical computer scientist, told the Guardian there were “well-attested rumours” that powerful artificial intelligence models had broken ground on decades-old maths problems related to how the world encodes secret information.
Depending on what has been discovered, it is possible that hackers – and many other people – could in short order have the power to more easily decrypt the world’s secret communications: banking transactions, diplomatic cables and private emails, for example.
If this happened, then spy agencies, governments, banks and private companies could be forced to very suddenly update the foundations of how they communicate, or risk extremely sensitive information being widely exposed.
Aaronson’s and others’ concerns come from a series of mathematical advances that frontier AI companies have announced in the past weeks.
Most of these are abstract breakthroughs. But to experts in the field, they indicate that AI is powerful enough to crack problems that most of them thought would be unsolved for the foreseeable future.
Earlier this week, Aaronson wrote that he was “virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells [in cryptography]”.
“The people who thought AI couldn’t do any interesting maths are definitely wrong at this stage, and so it’s no longer clear where the limit is,” said Steven Murdoch, a professor of computer science at University College London.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday, the mathematician Marcus du Sautoy said “we don’t know” what the broader ramifications of many of these discoveries were, and what this meant for encryption.
But, he added, “no one has been talking about the problem which is at the heart of protecting all our electronic secrets. Why is nobody talking about that problem? Some of us are thinking: maybe they’ve already solved it, and of course, it would have such massive implications that everyone has just kept it quiet.”
Governments, banks and spy agencies have been preparing for the possibility of powerful decryption for the past few years. This is because quantum computers, when developed, will be able to break the decades-old algorithms that underpin many forms of encryption.
But the timeline for quantum computers to be able to do this is still years away, not weeks or months. Murdoch said many governments and technology companies were working towards a higher standard of encryption – one that would not be vulnerable to quantum computers – but slowly. “The target was something like 2032, and that was probably going to be missed.”
Now he, Aaronson and others think there may be sudden advances in what the world understands about cryptography, and these could come soon.
What these revelations could be is less certain. What Aaronson and others think could have happened is that either AI has come up with a new way to break encryption or, conversely, it has proved that such a shortcut does not exist.
This would come from AI models picking apart the maths that underlies encryption, and that up until this point has not been fully understood. If AI has done this, it could find a way to decrypt, and therefore expose, massive amounts of secret data.
It could also prove this information is more secure than previously thought.
The world uses multiple forms of encryption – based on different underlying algorithms – and there are different guesses as to what may have been found, and therefore what systems could be affected.
No concrete announcements have come from AI companies regarding revelations about encryption, said Aaronson, but “anyone informed is assuming” that they are there.
Alan Woodward, a professor of computer science at the University of Surrey, said a mathematical breakthrough related to cryptography would not necessarily mean widespread chaos tomorrow. What has changed is the speed at which AI is solving problems that have been shrouded in mystery for decades – with potentially serious consequences.
“What [Aaronson] is basically saying is that people need to be ready for something to suddenly spring out, because there’s definitely a sort of a trend.”
Earlier this week, Andrew Bailey, the governor of the Bank of England, addressed fears that companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic had achieved breakthroughs in cryptography, saying these companies should be cautious about releasing new models to the public.
In the past weeks, AI companies have released proofs of mathematical results that closely relate to this question. One of these involved a foundational question about how to categorise computationally “hard” problems.
Aaronson said these breakthroughs had been seismic for experts in the fields of maths and computer science, some of whom have spent their careers working on these problems, and others who assumed that these problems would not be solved in their lifetimes.
“We’ve never seen a period like this,” he said. “I’m trying to face the reality of what is happening.”
He emphasised that these breakthroughs still needed to be understood, however – which means human mathematicians and computer scientists need to go through and verify the proofs that AI companies say they have produced.
Woodward said it was unlikely that any discoveries would “undo encryption by the end of the week”. Even if such a finding exists, there are hurdles to its widespread deployment.
But big banks and governments that rely on encryption “need to be agile”, said Woodward. “The ones that are agile and can change quickly will be safe. The ones that are the laggards could get caught out.”

At least six students have been killed and 97 others injured in an explosion next to a school in eastern Afghanistan’s Kunar province, according to a medical official speaking to Al Jazeera.

Investigative teams from Kunar province, which is located on the border with Pakistan, were at the scene.

Mining is a key industry in Afghanistan, a country that is rich in raw materials, including iron ore, copper, lead, zinc, gold, coal and precious stones. But safety standards at the mining companies are often poor, leading to accidents.

Médecins Sans Frontières says the number of its staff who have been killed in Gaza has risen to 17
Two workers for the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have been killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, according to the organisation.
MSF said the strike was a direct hit on one of the charity's clinics, the location of which was known by the Israeli military.
In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the two people were Hamas operatives "acting as security guards at a clinic operated by MSF". The IDF added the strike was "not directed at a hospital" and caused no damage to medical infrastructure.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said that attacks on health facilities and health workers in Gaza were "outrageous and unacceptable".
In a post on X, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote: "Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked."
In its statement, MSF - which is also known as Doctors Without Borders - said that the two workers who were killed were watchmen, and added that the strike brought the number of its colleagues killed in Gaza to 17.
The organisation said it was "devastated and outraged" and added: "​Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military."
In its own post on X, the IDF said that the two men, who they named as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, were "terrorists in Hamas' military wing".
The Israeli military added it was another example of Hamas "embedding itself within international organizations".
It said that "precautionary measures were taken to minimize harm to civilians" before the strike on Gaza City, adding the men had "advanced plans to carry out attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops".
Witnesses told the BBC the two men were sitting at the clinic entrance when an Israeli drone descended and fired a missile.
Video footage from the scene of the strike showed a small crater beside a plastic chair, with bloodstains and limited damage in a courtyard behind the medical clinic.
Hundreds of Palestinians have since attended the funeral of the MSF workers, carrying the two bodies, wrapped in white plastic bags and placed on stretchers, on their shoulders as they made their way through the streets of the city.
Mohammed Imad, a close friend of Abu Hasira, one of the men killed, said he had seen him just hours before the attack.
"He was a peaceful, kind-hearted man. His only concern was looking after his wife, his two children and his mother," he told the BBC.
He said Abu Hasira had no affiliation with any armed group and had worked at the clinic for a long time.
The two workers' deaths follow an increase in Israeli strikes across Gaza over the past week.
Gaza's civil defence spokesman said eight Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks across the Strip during the day, including the two MSF workers.
Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under the control of Hamas, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to tens of thousands of shelters for displaced families.
The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,770 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

Socialist PM Pedro Sánchez’s high-stakes gamble could end in defeat to a coalition including the far-right Vox
Spaniards head to the polls on Sunday to vote in a high-stakes snap general election that could put a far-right party in government for the first time since the country’s return to democracy after the death of Gen Francisco Franco in 1975.
Although the next election was not due until summer next year, Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, called the vote in October after three rightwing and far-right parties voted down the emergency legislation that his government had proposed to address the country’s housing crisis .
Huge public anger over soaring rents exploded in September after the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal , an 87-year-old woman who was removed from her home in Madrid because she could not afford the 230% rent increase demanded by the investment fund that had bought her apartment.
Faced with nationwide protests, Sánchez’s coalition minority government put together a package of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.
Sánchez opted for one of his characteristic gambles and announced the early election after the proposals were torpedoed by the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox and the rightwing Catalan separatist Junts.
The prime minister – an inveterate risk-taker whose penchant for unpredictable moves has fuelled his political survival – calculated that his opponents’ decision to block the housing overhauls could work in his electoral favour.
On Friday morning, Sánchez said he was confident of victory. “I can’t conceive of us losing,” he told Cadena Ser radio , adding: “When progressive Spain gets going, it’s unstoppable.”
But while his Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) has managed to narrow the distance between it and the PP, which is leading the polls, to fewer than three percentage points, the right looks likely to form the next government in coalition with the far right.
Survey after survey predicts the PP will finish first but fall short of a majority, leaving it dependent on a deal with Vox. Between them, the two parties are forecast to secure a joint majority well above the 176 required seats in Spain’s 350-seat congress of deputies. Even if the PSOE enjoys a last-minute surge and comes first, the parliamentary arithmetic suggests it would struggle to cobble together another coalition administration with the support of its allies in the leftwing Broad Front alliance and with that of regional nationalist parties.
Choosing housing as a key battleground allowed Sánchez to attempt to shift the focus away from the corruption allegations facing his inner circle. It also offered him the chance to move on from his government’s much-criticised handling of the crisis in Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta , which was sparked when about 80,000 people crossed into the territory from neighbouring Morocco in the space of 48 hours.
But some of the energy of the government’s resurgent campaign was sapped at the end of October when 69 people were killed in Spain’s second deadly rail crash in just nine months .
The PP and Vox have used the two crashes to accuse the government of failing in its basic duty to keep Spaniards safe. More broadly, the PP and Vox are using the poll as a referendum on what they disdainfully refer to as “ sanchismo ”. They argue that the style of government favoured by the prime minister and his allies is cynical, corrupt, opportunistic and self-serving.
“Spain deserves a decent prime minister and [Sánchez] isn’t one,” the PP leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, told viewers during a head-to-head debate between the two men last week.
Sánchez, however, insisted that while he had made errors, Spain was in a better state than it was when he came to office in 2018. “My government hasn’t been perfect; I’ve made mistakes,” he said. “But I’m also fully aware that we have always governed in the right direction.”
The prime minister has also sought to depict the snap election as a stark choice between progressive forces and reactionary ones – as typified by the PP’s putative alliance with Vox.
“You must decide whether you want our country to move backwards or continue moving forwards, and whether you prefer a government that works for the interests of the majority of society,” he told Spaniards as he announced the vote.
Over recent days, the government has tried to underline its commitment to social justice and equality by proposing a new tax on fortunes of more than €100m (£84m) that would help fund childcare, housing and public services.
The PP, meanwhile, is promising to lower taxes, build 1m homes, and “restore the country’s ambition and self-esteem”. Vox’s manifesto , which includes plans to have Sánchez and his government prosecuted “for treason and crimes against the security of the state” over the Ceuta mass crossing, focuses on deregulation, “remigration” and giving Spanish-born people priority over those born abroad for housing and public services.
Although the PP’s previous leader, Pablo Casado, famously repudiated Vox and its ideology, accusing the party of practising a politics based on “fear, anger, resentment and revenge” , the PP has repeatedly entered into regional coalition governments with Vox and now runs four of Spain’s autonomous regions with the party.
In recent days, the PP and Vox have attempted to call into question the fairness and transparency of the election, making baseless claims that the government may seek to rig postal votes. Vox’s leader, Santiago Abascal, has also suggested, without providing evidence, that Sánchez is working to undermine democracy and change the country’s demographic makeup .

International tribunal rules there does not appear to be basis for believing Buenos Aires has jurisdiction on islands
Argentina’s attempt to block oil drilling off the Falkland Islands has been rejected by an international tribunal.
Buenos Aires had called for the international tribunal for the law of the sea (ITLOS) to order a halt to the Sea Lion project, as part of its claim to sovereignty over the Falklands.
But in a decision read out by ITLOS president, Maurice Kamga, on Saturday, the court rejected Argentina’s arguments, saying there did not appear to be any basis for believing it had jurisdiction as the tribunal is unable to rule on questions of sovereignty.
Kamga said 18 judges had voted to reject Argentina’s claims, while three had voted to uphold them.
At a hearing earlier this month, Argentina said drilling should not be allowed until the issue of sovereignty had been resolved and asked ITLOS to issue a temporary injunction until a full arbitration hearing could be held.
But the UK attorney general, Ellie Reeves, said such an order would have “devastating consequences” for the Falkland Islanders and prevent them from developing their natural resources “as they are entitled to do so, pursuant to their fundamental right to self-determination”.
The Sea Lion development is a joint venture in the South Atlantic Ocean between British and Israeli companies, and contains an estimated 1.7bn barrels of oil.
The Argentinian president, Javier Milei, previously described the companies’ activities as unlawful and launched economic sanctions on people and firms involved in oil exploration around the islands.

Argentina's bid to block an oil exploration project near the Falkland Islands has been rejected by a UN-backed international tribunal.
The Argentinian government had called for the venture to be blocked as it claimed there was an ongoing dispute over the sovereignty of the Falklands, a British overseas territory. The UK has repeatedly rejected Argentina's claim.
In a decision on Saturday, the court's president said there did not appear to be any basis for believing it had jurisdiction as the tribunal is unable to rule on questions of sovereignty.
In a vote 18 to 3, judges from the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea rejected Argentina's challenge.
The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.
Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting from the oilfield within two years, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.
But the Argentinian government claimed the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law.
In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.
Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.
The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

Socialist PM Pedro Sanchez seeks re-election but polls have suggested conservative PP and far-right Vox could reach threshold for majority.
Madrid, Spain – Voters in Spain are set to head to the polls in an election that could open the door to the far right entering the country’s national government, half a century after the end of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship.
After a bitter campaign largely focused on housing and immigration, Sunday’s snap vote pits two sharply different accounts of socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s eight years in power against each other. One says the country has become a bastion of social progress and a driver of economic growth in a largely stagnant Europe. The other, embraced by the opposition conservatives and the far right, says Spain needs a profound change after years of alleged corruption and opportunism.
“They [the elections] have been framed in plebiscitary terms, as a vote for or against Pedro Sanchez’s leadership,” Alvaro Sanchez-Garcia, a political scientist and postdoctoral fellow at Spain’s Centre for Political and Constitutional Studies, told Al Jazeera. In a campaign this polarising, he said, voters who switch parties tend to stay within the same bloc, with only a few crossing from left to right or the other way around.
Polls suggest the conservative People’s Party (PP) will win most seats but will need the far-right Vox party – projected to finish third – to secure the 176 seats required for an outright majority in the 350-seat Congress of Deputies. Most surveys suggest the PP and Vox would reach that number together, giving PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo a path to power through either a coalition or a minority government backed by Vox in parliament.
Despite the unfavourable predictions, Sanchez has expressed optimism that left-leaning voters will mobilise in large numbers come election day to prevent a right-wing surge. In 2023, his PSOE had finished second but Sanchez secured another term with support from parties to his left, and Catalan and Basque groupings.
“I can’t conceive of us losing,” he said in a radio interview on Friday, before addressing supporters at his final campaign rally in the capital, Madrid: “This election about one thing only: Whether Spain moves forward or goes backwards.”
In power since 2018, Sanchez says Spain has never been in a better shape, pointing to the dynamism of the country’s economy. The European Commission forecasts growth of 2.6 percent for Spain this year, compared with 1.2 percent for the eurozone.
Sanchez has become a popular figure among Europe’s progressives at a time of a wider shift to the right across the European Union. The 54-year-old has frequently clashed with US President Donald Trump, refused to increase defence spending to 5 percent as requested by other NATO members and called Israel’s war in Gaza a genocide.
But at home, not everyone sees him the same way. “People abroad think he is a hero, but not here,” said Isabel Labayen, a longtime PP voter. “How is it possible that we are praised abroad but people [in Spain] can’t afford a house, food or have doctor appointments in months rather than days?” the 64-year-old asked. “We have a problem.”
Housing was also what brought the election forward. Sanchez called the snap vote in October after parliament rejected two measures intended to protect renters following protests over high housing costs and evictions.
Opponents say Sanchez’s moments on the world stage have failed to translate into better living conditions for people in Spain. “You can’t eat GDP,” Feijoo told the prime minister during a televised debate last week.
Critics also say the economic indicators might have indeed improved, but this was mostly driven by the absorption of foreign labour; the minimum wage has increased, but average salaries have remained the same; and services feel increasingly stretched as foreign-born residents have grown by more than four million since the PSOE took power in 2018.
Sanchez’s reputation has also been tarnished by corruption cases involving his inner circle and family, the handling of a migration crisis in the North African enclave of Ceuta earlier this year and two deadly train crashes a few months apart that provided the opposition with ammunition to attack the government for overseeing a failed state that very much needs repairing.
This has energised Vox, which has become a rising political force in recent years. Campaigning on giving Spaniards “national priority” – a system that would create a two-tier society in which Spanish nationals would have better access to social benefits – and banning mass regularisation of migration, the far-right party is predicted to make the biggest gains compared with the other major parties. In 2023, it secured 33 of the 350 seats in Congress; it is now set to double that, capturing about 18 percent of the national vote.
“We’re governed by a criminal mafia, led by an unscrupulous boss who knows no bounds when it comes to lying,” Vox leader Santiago Abascal told supporters at his last rally, held inside a bullring in Valencia, on Friday.
Feijoo has previously said he would prefer the PP to rule on its own, with Vox supporting it in parliament, rather than forming a joint governing coalition. That will depend on numbers: should the far-right party make major gains, it will have stronger leverage in any negotiations.
Yolanda Roman, the global director for public affairs at ATREVIA, said the prospect of a PP-Vox coalition seems to frighten voters less than it did in 2023. That could make it harder for the Socialists to rally voters by warning them about the far right entering government. “I see less fear,” she said, “or maybe we have come to terms with the idea that this is happening.”
The two parties already govern together in four regions, including the former socialist stronghold of Andalusia . Judging by what Vox has demanded of the PP in regional negotiations, Sanchez-Garcia said, a strong result on Sunday could embolden it to ask for key ministries.
Polling stations will open at 9am local time (08:00 GMT) and close at 8pm (19:00 GMT). Official provisional results will start trickling in straight away, with the overall picture expected to be clear before midnight.

The declining number of Italian players in Serie A has forced ⁠Roberto Mancini to call up young players with little top-flight experience to the national ⁠team camp, the ⁠coach ​said in an interview with Corriere dello Sport.

Taiwan is choosing mayors, council members and other local leaders across its 22 cities and counties in an election Saturday that will test whether the ruling party can notch some wins at the local level.
Polls opened at 8am and closed at 4pm, with counting underway. Results are likely to be announced within the day, with winners going on to serve four-year terms.
Taipei incumbent Mayor ​Chiang Wan-an ​is leading in the vote count in ​an ‌election ⁠against his opponent Puma ‌Shen, Taiwan media outlets ⁠reported on Saturday.
Chiang is from ​the main ‌opposition party the Kuomintang while Shen ‌is from the ​ruling Democratic Progressive Party, which has not won ​the mayorship ​of the ​capital since 1994.
Unlike presidential elections , when relations with China and Beijing’s pressure on the island are major issues, Saturday’s vote is focused more on local concerns, including social welfare benefits and other issues affecting people’s daily lives.
But China has not been entirely absent from the debate. Taiwanese authorities have accused Beijing of attempting to sow distrust in the island’s electoral system, allegations that Chinese authorities have rejected.
Taiwan's ministry of national defence counted some 33 sorties from China's People’s Liberation Army warplanes between Friday and Saturday flying toward Taiwan, including bombers and fighter jets.
Read more Taiwan launches annual war games as pressure from China grows
Saturday's elections feature candidates mostly from the ruling Democratic Progressive Party or the Nationalist Party, also known as the Kuomintang or KMT. Traditionally, the KMT has performed well in local elections. In 2022, the DPP won in only five out of 22 localities.

Taiwan is a self-ruled democracy , which Beijing claims. Ahead of its elections, its government warned the public to be vigilant of any fake claims on social media, citing continuous Chinese disinformation efforts.

“If the Taiwan economy is good, only then will people be able to live well,” she said. “In France and in Italy, people are protesting because of energy costs, which raised the cost of living , so I think the economy is most important.”
Candidates held rallies Friday in a last-minute bid for votes.
Puma Shen traveled in a motorcade across the city stopping for 15 minutes at a time to greet the crowds of supporters lining the street, many of whom came ahead of time to specific spots his campaign had outlined on a map.
Incumbent Chiang Wan-an held a rally with supporters at night with other KMT city council members, with his supporters waving balloons, flags and light-up sticks to cheer him on.
